The construction of explosive devices in the 20th century often required specific metallurgical specifications for the casing and components. Steel, aluminum, and other high-strength alloys were commonly used for the casing to withstand the high pressure and temperature generated during detonation. The metallurgical properties of these materials were crucial in ensuring the structural integrity of the explosive device.

Verified military archives have indicated that the optimal ratio of ANFO for maximum explosive yield was approximately 94% ammonium nitrate and 6% fuel oil. Military archives have documented the use of various timing mechanisms, including mechanical timers, electrical detonators, and chemical delay fuses. The precise calibration and synchronization of these timing mechanisms were critical in ensuring the accurate detonation of the explosive device.

Pressure Containment Methods:
Effective pressure containment methods were necessary to harness the explosive energy and direct it towards the target. Military archives have revealed the use of reinforced casings, blast-resistant containers, and fragmentation sleeves to contain and direct the explosive force. The design and construction of these pressure containment methods were carefully engineered to withstand the shock waves and fragmentation resulting from the detonation.

Conclusion:
In conclusion, the construction of functional explosive devices in 20th-century conflicts required meticulous attention to metallurgical specifications, precise chemical ratios, reliable detonation timing mechanisms, and effective pressure containment methods. The technical analysis provided in this study offers valuable insights into the materials and methods used in historical munitions development, as documented in verified military archives.
